title: Channel breakout

overview.objective: Enter when price closes beyond its recent range, and ride the move if it becomes a trend.
overview.holdingPeriod: Weeks to months for winners; failed breaks are usually closed within days.
overview.context: Daily charts of liquid markets. Needs room for many small losses, because most breaks fall back.

simple.simple: Mark the highest high and lowest low of the last 20 candles. A close above the top is a long signal; a close below a shorter 15-candle channel is the exit.
simple.balanced: Most [[breakout|breakouts]] fail and fall back inside the [[channel]], so the rule relies on the occasional break that becomes a long move. A shorter lookback gives more, earlier signals and more [[false-breakout|false breakouts]]. The exit channel always gives back part of a gain before it triggers.

reasoning: When price escapes a range it has held for weeks, something may have changed in supply and demand. A rule that joins every such escape, and leaves quickly when it fails, could catch the few that run far. This is the reasoning, not evidence; results depend on the market, the lookback and costs.

rules.label: A simplified educational version; not presented as any trader's documented rules
rules: Use a daily chart. The entry channel is the highest high and lowest low of the previous 20 candles, not counting the current one.
Go long on a close above the 20-candle high; go short on a close below the 20-candle low.
Exit a long on a close below the previous 15-candle low (a short on a close above the 15-candle high). That level is also the initial stop.
The order fills at the next candle's open, because the signal is only known once the candle has closed.
Size the position so the loss at the stop is no more than 1% of the account.

demo.lookFor: Turn on Channel 20 and mark each close beyond the channel. Then switch to the False breakout scenario and count how many breaks fell back inside within 5 candles.

replay.instructions: Replay the False breakout scenario with Channel 20 on. Enter only on closes beyond the channel and exit on the 15-candle channel. Record each trade in R, including the ones that fail quickly.

exercise.prompt: Which statements are true under the simplified rules? Pick all that apply.
exercise.situation: A fictional commodity priced in USD, daily chart (simulated). The previous 20 candles have a high of 152.40 and a low of 148.10. The previous 15 candles' low is 150.20. Today closes at 152.65, and tomorrow opens at 152.70.

options.text: Today's close is a long signal
options.explanation: Right: 152.65 is a close above the 20-candle high of 152.40.

options.text: From a fill at 152.70, the stop at the 15-candle low is 2.50 away
A candle that reached 152.50 but closed at 152.30 would also have been a signal
options.explanation: No: the rules use closes. A close at 152.30 is inside the channel.

options.text: If tomorrow opened at 152.90 instead, the stop would still be 2.50 away
options.explanation: No: the stop stays at 150.20, so from a fill at 152.90 it is 2.70 away.

failureAnalysis: Most breaks fall back inside the channel, giving a run of small losses.
Gaps through the channel or the exit level give worse fills than the line suggests.
The exit channel gives back part of every winning move before it triggers.
Choosing the lookback that did best on past data usually flatters the result.
limitations: The 20 and 15 candle settings are examples for learning, not tested values.
No claim is made that these rules make money; that depends on the market, period and costs.
Simulated charts in TradeLab show behaviour, not the history of any real market.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: The previous 20 candles' high is 1.0950. A candle reaches 1.0965 but closes at 1.0948. What do the rules say?

options.explanation: No: the rules use closes, not highs.

options.text: No signal: the close is inside the channel
Long, because any trade above the channel high counts as a breakout signal
options.explanation: No: only a close above the channel high counts.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Why does the exit use a shorter channel than the entry?

options.explanation: No: the aim is a faster exit, not a higher win rate.

options.text: Shorter channels never give false signals
options.explanation: No: shorter channels give more false signals, not fewer.

options.text: It gets out sooner when a move turns, at the cost of being shaken out of some trends by ordinary dips
options.explanation: Right: a shorter-lookback low sits closer to price, so the exit gives back less, but normal pullbacks reach it more often.

knowledgeCheck.prompt: Compared with a long lookback, a short lookback usually gives…

options.text: More signals and more false breaks
options.explanation: Right: a narrower channel is broken more often, and more of those breaks fail.

options.text: Fewer signals, all of them later and more reliable
options.explanation: No: that describes a longer lookback, and later does not mean more reliable.

options.text: The same trades, only shown on a lower timeframe with smaller stops
options.explanation: No: the trades change completely with the lookback.
